title: Radioactive Decay and the Geologic Time Scale
learningObjectives: Explain how the discovery of radioactivity makes it possible to calculate numeric ages of rocks in years
Define half-life as the time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms
Describe how isotopic techniques measure when a mineral within a rock was formed using parent-to-daughter decay

explanations.text: Numeric ages for rocks can be calculated in years because minerals containing naturally occurring radioactive elements decay at a measurable rate. This discovery made it possible to assign ages in thousands, millions and billions of years.

evidence.quote: The assignment of ages of rocks in thousands, millions, and billions of years was made possible by the discovery of radioactivity.
Now we can use minerals that contain naturally occurring radioactive elements to calculate the numeric age of a rock in years.

explanations.text: The decay of a parent isotope to a daughter isotope occurs at a constant rate described by the half-life. Each radioactive isotope has its own unique half-life, which is the time needed for half of the parent atoms to decay.

evidence.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.
Each radioactive isotope has its own unique half-life.

explanations.text: Isotopic techniques determine when a mineral formed by measuring remaining parent atoms and newly produced daughter atoms, allowing numeric ages to be correlated with the fossil-based relative time scale.

evidence.quote: Isotopic techniques are used to measure the time at which a particular mineral within a rock was formed.
The basic unit of each chemical element is the atom.
